responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character13_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well… I reckon if you asked Character13_M about fairness, he’d say it’s about getting a square deal—no special treatment, but no getting stepped on either. He always talked about how when he was younger, folks worked hard and expected to get by on that alone. Not rich, mind you, but able to pay the bills, keep a roof overhead, maybe take the family camping once a summer. Fairness, to him, meant that effort should count for something. That you shouldn’t watch someone who didn’t play by the rules end up ahead of you—not because you hate them, but because it makes you feel like the game’s rigged.

Belonging? That was deeper for him. He grew up in a neighborhood where everyone knew each other—the mailman, the guy at the gas station, the kids playing stickball in the street. His dad came back from Korea, got a job at the plant, stayed there 35 years. There was a rhythm to life, a kind of unspoken understanding: you looked out for your block, you respected your elders, you went to church or the VFW hall not just for ceremony, but because it meant you were *part* of something. Belonging wasn’t given—it was earned through showing up, through consistency.

Community, to him, wasn’t just geography. It was shared experience. He’d often say, “You don’t build community with slogans. You build it over fence lines, in diner booths, at union meetings.” He worried, especially later in life, that people were losing that—that everyone was glued to screens, moving fast, living isolated. He didn’t blame immigrants for that—but he did worry that when too much changes too fast, the glue holding neighborhoods together starts to crack.

One thing he told me once stuck with me: “I ain’t scared of different. I’m scared of disconnected.” He saw a lot of new faces in town—some from Latin America, others from Africa, some speaking languages he couldn’t place. He didn’t resent that, not really. But he *did* wonder—if they’re not learning our ways, and we’re not trying to understand theirs—where does the common ground come in? Where’s the middle?

He believed belonging had to go both ways. You welcome people in, sure—but they’ve got to want to be *in*, not just live alongside. And fairness? That cuts both ways too. He felt locals deserved consideration—especially working folks just scraping by—when it came to jobs, schools, services. He didn’t see that as selfish. He saw it as responsibility.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character13_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*[Sitting back a little, voice low and steady, like he’s actually there in the garden]*

Well… I’m sittin’ here on this old bench—same one they’ve had since the ‘80s, wood a little splintered now—and I look around, and it’s… different than it used to be. Not bad. Just *different*.

Over by the tomato plots, there’s Maria and her grandson, digging in the soil same as me. She came from Guatemala, been here twenty years. Speaks English fine but still switches when she’s excited. She brings tamales every Thanksgiving to the shed out back, even though we never asked. That’s neighborly. That’s *community*. And across the way, Mr. Ibrahim—he’s from Somalia, wears that knit cap year-round—always nods at me, asks how my hip’s doin’. Polite. Respectful. I appreciate that.

But then there’s others—like that fella in Unit 6, always loud late at night, music blarin’, sometimes people comin’ and goin’ who don’t live here. Smells like weed, sometimes worse. Landlord won’t do nothin’. And down near the back gate, there’s that couple—unmarried, live together, which ain’t my business—but they fight something fierce, and half the time you hear it through the walls. Or the young guy who just got out of rehab, stumbling home some nights, reeking of cheap wine. I feel bad for him, truly—but is it fair to the families with kids trying to sleep?

So yeah, I see all kinds. And I’ll tell ya—I don’t mind the skin color, the accent, the religion. Never did. What matters to me is: do you respect the place? Do you pitch in? Do you keep your word?

Back when I worked at the warehouse, we had fellas from Puerto Rico, from Poland, even a Greek guy who barely spoke English. But we got along because we all showed up on time, pulled our weight, didn’t cause trouble. We looked out for each other. That’s what I miss—*that kind of mixing*, where difference doesn’t mean division.

Now sometimes it feels like… folks are just stacked on top of each other, not woven together. Like threads that don’t knot.

I’ll talk to anyone. I’ve learned “buenos días,” I say “salaam” when Mr. Ibrahim greets me. But I also think—some folks come here and never learn English. Never show up at meetings. Don’t join the cleanup days. And the city pours money into translating signs, hiring interpreters, but the potholes go unfilled and the rec center’s closed.

That’s when fairness starts to itch. Not because they’re foreign. But because *we’re all supposed to be in this together*—and it don’t always feel that way.

So my feeling? I want to welcome people. I really do. But welcome means two-way streets. You let me in your life a little, I’ll let you in mine. Otherwise, we’re just strangers sharing dirt.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*[Leans forward, hands on knees, voice a little quieter—like he’s choosing words carefully]*

Look… I grew up in a time when things were simpler—or at least, they *seemed* simpler. Folks kept to certain norms. You married young, went to church, didn’t talk much about personal troubles. But I’ve lived long enough now to know life ain’t clean lines.

I’ve seen good men go down hard from drink—my own brother, God rest him. Lost him to the bottle at 62. So when I see someone stumbling home late, reeking of whiskey? Yeah, it bothers me. But more than that, it *hurts*. Because I know what’s underneath. I don’t judge that man—I worry about him. Same with the ones using pills or worse. That’s not “bad people”—that’s pain. And if we’re gonna call ourselves a community, we can’t just shut the door on pain.

Now, about diseases—HIV, hepatitis, whatever—it’s scary, sure. I’ll admit, when I first heard about AIDS back in the ’80s, I didn’t understand it. Thought it was something far away, something that only happened to “those kinds” of people. But then my nephew’s partner died from it. Real close. And I learned. Learned it ain’t about lifestyle—it’s about health. And if someone’s sick, they need care, not shame. We’ve got clinics, we’ve got programs. We should use ‘em. Compassion doesn’t mean ignoring risk—but it does mean treating folks like humans, not outcasts.

As for different backgrounds—skin color, language, religion—I’ve said it before: I don’t fear difference. I fear *disrespect*. I had a coworker, Ramon, came here from El Salvador. Spoke Spanish mostly at first. Boss put him on night shift every time—figure he wouldn’t mind, being an immigrant and all. I spoke up. Said, “He’s got kids too. He deserves weekends off like the rest of us.” We became friends. His daughter even called me “Tío Frank” after a while. That’s how you build trust—not by ignoring differences, but by standing *with* someone when it counts.

Now, the unmarried couples—living together, gay, straight, whatever—I’ll be honest: it took me some years. Grew up Catholic, you know how it is. But then I met Sarah, over at the food pantry. She’s raising two kids with her partner, Lisa. They volunteer every Tuesday. Work hard. Pay taxes. Love those kids more than anything. After a while, I asked myself: *What exactly am I holding against them?* That they love differently? No. Can’t do that. Not if I want to sleep at night with a clear conscience.

So yeah—tolerance? It’s needed most where fear lives. And fear usually comes from not knowing. From silence. From never sitting across the table.

The reason I push for more talk—more real talk—is because I’ve seen what happens when we don’t. Neighborhoods turn cold. People retreat. The addicts suffer alone. The newcomers stay strangers. The angry ones start blaming.

But if we actually *talk*—not yelling, not on Facebook—if we sit, face-to-face, and say, “This is who I am. This is what I carry”—then maybe, just maybe, we find common ground.

Comfort doesn’t come from everyone being the same. It comes from knowing you won’t be crushed for being different.

And that? That’s something worth building. Even if it’s slow. Even if it’s hard.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character13_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*[Sighs, rubs his knee like it’s bothering him—voice a little heavier now]*

Fairness… when there ain’t enough to go around? That’s the real test, isn’t it?

I’ll tell you straight—I worked 42 years. Started at a loading dock, ended up in maintenance. Never made big money, but I showed up. Rain, snow, flu season—I was there. My pension? Peanuts now. Social Security barely covers rent and meds. So when I see jobs—*real jobs*, not just gig work or cash under the table—going to folks who just got here, while guys I know, good workers, are sitting at home watching daytime TV… that stings.

Now don’t get me wrong—I’m not saying immigrants don’t work hard. Hell, some of ‘em put in twice the hours I ever did. But here’s where fairness gets bent: when the system lets employers bring in temporary workers—cheaper, easier to push around—while local people, especially older ones, get told, “You’re overqualified,” or “We need younger energy.” That ain’t fair. That’s using immigration as a shortcut to lower wages.

And let’s talk about the industries. I’ve seen farms hire crews from Mexico—fine, if they’re paid right, treated right. But too often? They’re living ten to a trailer, scared to complain, no benefits, no voice. And the boss likes that. Keeps costs down. Meanwhile, American-born guys—Black, white, doesn’t matter—are told there’s “no work.” But there *is* work—just not for them.

So what’s the balance?

First—**local first**. If we’ve got working folks in this town, county, state—who’ve paid taxes, raised families, served in one way or another—they oughta get first shot at jobs when times are lean. Not because they’re “better,” but because they’ve *been here*, invested in the place. That’s loyalty. That deserves something.

Second—**no undercutting**. If a migrant worker comes in, great—but they should be paid the same wage, have the same rights, the same safety rules. No loopholes. No “they’ll take less” nonsense. That only drags everybody down. Union halls used to protect that. Now? Feels like everyone’s on their own.

Third—**skills matter, but so does time**. I get that some new folks bring trades, languages, energy. Good. We need that. But don’t act like a 50-year-old mechanic with bad knees is useless. He knows things. He’s reliable. He won’t steal from the warehouse. That counts.

And fourth—**don’t flood the well**. I’ve seen towns where the factory brings in 200 guest workers, builds barracks for ‘em, but closes the day care for local kids. Where schools strain, ERs back up, buses overcrowd—and locals feel like strangers in their own town. That breeds anger. Not because people hate immigrants—but because they feel *replaced*, not included.

So balance? It’s gotta be managed. Not open door, not closed fist. You bring people in—yes—but slowly. With planning. With respect for both sides.

And above all? **No pitting us against each other**. That’s what kills fairness. When bosses, or politicians, play the “you vs. them” game—locals vs. migrants—it’s always the little guy who loses. They want us fighting each other so they can keep cutting wages, breaking unions, dodging responsibility.

Fairness means seeing *all* working people as in the same boat—even if we got here different ways.

And if we’re gonna fix things, we gotta row together. Not throw folks overboard to make the boat lighter.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character13_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*[Leans back, looks off toward the horizon like he's weighing each word]*

You ask me about all these different views on immigration—national level stuff—and I’ll tell you: most of ‘em got *some* truth to ‘em. Not all, but enough that we oughta listen instead of just yell.

First—the ones who say immigrants fill jobs we can’t or won’t do? That’s *partly* true. I ain’t gonna pretend every farm hand, meatpacker, or overnight janitor is some exploitable foreigner. But let’s be real: a lot of Americans don’t want those jobs—not for the pay, not for the hours. I worked tough jobs, but I also saw when work got too dangerous, too dirty, and folks started quitting. And yeah, new people came in. Sometimes legally, sometimes not. But here’s what gets left out: **why** don’t people want those jobs? Because they don’t pay enough. Because there’s no way up. So instead of blaming immigrants for “taking” them, maybe we fix the jobs. Pay fair wages. Make ‘em safe. Then see who wants ‘em.

Now, this talk about cultural diversity being a strength—I hear it. At festivals, at school plays, even at the diner where they added tamales and jerk chicken to the menu—there’s life in that. It keeps things from getting stale. My grandkids love music, food, styles from everywhere. I don’t always get it, but I see it makes ‘em curious, open. That’s good. But—and this is a big *but*—diversity only works if there’s a *shared center*. If everyone’s celebrating their own thing but nobody agrees on the basics—like language, laws, respect for institutions—then you don’t got vitality. You got fragments. And fragments break apart.

Then there’s the fear side—crime, security, terrorism. Now, I won’t lie—I worry about that too. Especially after everything on the news. But here’s what I’ve learned: most immigrants aren’t criminals. In fact, study after study says they commit crimes at *lower* rates than native-born. I didn’t wanna believe that at first—I thought, “They’re hiding something.” But then I looked into it. Talked to a guy at the sheriff’s office. He said, “Most of ‘em are trying to stay *under* the radar, not draw attention. They’re scared stiff of getting deported.” So the idea that every newcomer’s a threat? That’s fear talk, not fact talk.

But… and this is important… **the exceptions stick in your mind**. One cartel guy caught in our state. One refugee involved in an attack five years ago. One neighborhood that changed fast—language, habits, even street signs—and folks felt lost. Those stories spread fast. They feel personal. And when leaders use ‘em to scare people? That poisons the well.

Humanitarian angle—helping refugees, people fleeing war or starvation—that hits me deep. I remember Vietnam. I remember Ethiopians in the ‘80s. Some made good lives. Some struggled. But turning away people in crisis? That don’t sit right with me as a Christian man. If my family had been starving, running from bombs—wouldn’t I want someone to open the door?

But—and again, there’s a *but*—you can’t save the whole world *without* thinking how it affects the people already here. Because if schools are overcrowded, clinics are backed up, housing prices go up, and your kid can’t get into community college because spots are filled—then you start asking: “Where’s *our* help?” Compassion’s got to have limits. Not heartless ones—but practical ones.

And then there’s the money fear—immigration driving down wages, taking jobs. I used to think that was just sour grapes. But now? I’ve seen it. Construction crews hiring cash-only guys who’ll work for less. Factories replacing retirees with H-2B visa workers. No benefits. No seniority. That *does* hurt working people. Especially older ones, or those without degrees. We don’t talk enough about how immigration policy gets used by business to keep labor cheap.

So what do I believe?

I believe:
- Immigrants *do* fill gaps—**but only because we let the gaps stay broken**.
- Diversity *can* enrich us—**but not if we lose common ground**.
- Security concerns *should be taken seriously*—**but not blown into blanket suspicion**.
- Humanitarian aid is *morally right*—**but must be managed, not endless**.
- Economic fears are *real for many people*—**and deserve honest answers, not mockery**.

What needs more facts? The crime stats. The wage studies. The long-term integration numbers. We need plain talk, not headlines. And dialogue? Yeah—we need to sit down. Locals, newcomers, faith leaders, workers. Not in Washington. In *our* towns. Over coffee. Ask: “What do you need? What are you afraid of? How can we make this work—for all of us?”

Because right now? Too many voices are shouting, and too few are listening.

And men like me—we’re not against immigrants. We’re against being forgotten.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character13_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*[Takes a slow breath, like he’s about to lay down a verdict he’s carried for years]*

Complete openness? No. As much as I believe in kindness, you can’t just throw the gates wide and say “come one, come all” when schools are underfunded, hospitals are short-staffed, and working folks are barely hanging on. That’s not generosity—that’s chaos. And chaos hurts the poor most of all, native-born *and* new.

Refusing entry altogether? That ain’t American. Never has been. My own granddaddy came from County Cork with nothing but a suitcase and a cough. They tested him, questioned him, made him wait—but they let him in. We don’t slam the door just because times get tough. That’s not who we are.

So between those two extremes? That’s where sense lives.

I’d go with **a mix—tight numbers, job-based first, with room for refugees, and real enforcement of rules**. Here’s how I see it:

First—**set clear, reasonable numerical limits**, based on what our towns, cities, and services can actually handle. Not some random number cooked up in D.C. Every ten years, take a look: How many new people can our schools absorb? Our clinics? Our housing? Then stick to it. Not a quota that gets ignored—*a promise*. And if we go over, fix it. Don’t just shrug.

Second—**prioritize workers where there’s honest shortages**, not just cheap labor. But—and this is key—those jobs gotta pay fair wages, have protections, offer a path. No more bringing in farmhands or meatpackers at poverty pay while American citizens sit idle. If the wage’s too low to attract local workers, *raise the wage*. Let the market work. If employers scream? Good. Maybe they’ll automate or improve conditions instead of leaning on desperation.

Third—**require integration, not just presence**. English language basics—not to shame anyone, but because you can’t be part of a community if you can’t talk to it. Civics too. What does the flag mean? What are your rights—and your responsibilities? Not a loyalty test. A welcome package. And yeah, kids pick it up fast—but adults need help too. Fund night classes. Use churches, libraries, VFW halls. Make it part of the deal.

Fourth—**keep a lane open for refugees**, but manage it. Not endless, not uncontrolled—but humane. We’ve got a moral duty to people fleeing war, torture, death threats. But we also owe stability to the people already here. So vet thoroughly. Resettle in stages. Support both the newcomers *and* the communities taking them in. No dumping folks in struggling neighborhoods without resources. That breeds resentment on both sides.

Fifth—**crack down on abuse—on all sides**. Employers hiring under the table to dodge taxes and wages? Fine ‘em heavy. Workers overstaying visas? There’s got to be consequences—maybe a chance to regularize, but not automatic amnesty every time. And for heaven’s sake, fix the backlogs. Folks playing by the rules waiting 15 years while others jump the line? That kills respect for the system.

And finally—**local input**. Let mayors, town councils, county boards have a real say in how many new residents they can absorb. Not total control—but a voice. Because the guy in Iowa doesn’t live what the guy in L.A. lives, and vice versa.

Fairness? It means no free rides—but no closed doors either.

Social integration? That don’t happen by accident. It takes effort. From them—and from us.

I want a policy that says: *We will welcome you—if you’re coming to stay, to work, to belong. Not to exploit, not to hide, not to replace us.* And we—the ones already here—we’ll meet you halfway. We’ll learn your name. Share a meal. But don’t ask us to disappear so you can take our place.

That’s the balance I’d strike.

Not perfect. But honest.  
Not easy. But fair.  
And above all—*American*.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character13_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character13_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*[Long pause. Takes off his cap, turns it in his hands, voice softer now—less character, more J reflecting through him]*

You know… I thought I knew Frank—Character13_M—pretty well. We went fishing, had coffee after church sometimes, argued about the Red Sox. But doing this—trying to *be* him, not just remember him—I saw something deeper.

I always figured his views on immigration came from being older, set in his ways, maybe a little suspicious of change. And yeah, there’s that. But what I really heard today—what *he* made me hear—is that it wasn’t fear of strangers that drove him. It was **fear of irrelevance**.

He didn’t want to be told his life’s work didn’t matter. That loyalty—to job, to neighborhood, to country—was outdated. He didn’t want new folks treated like they were better just for being new, or worse just for being different. He wanted *recognition*. That people like him—the quiet workers, the ones who paid taxes, showed up, kept their heads down—they still counted.

And honestly? That hit me.

Because I’ve been quicker to judge—people who say things like he did—as narrow-minded. I’d call it resistance. Now I see it’s also grief. Grief for a world that valued stability, where you could count on simple promises: work hard, play fair, stay put, belong.

But I also see clearer now where he fell short.

He talked about integration—but didn’t always see how hard it is to start over at 40 with three kids and no English. He worried about wages—but didn’t always connect how corporations use the system to weaken *all* workers, native and foreign-born alike. And while he had compassion—he carried it unevenly. Easier for the drunk neighbor than the undocumented one, even if both were hurting.

So this changed me.

Not that I agree with everything he believed. But I understand *why* he believed it. And that makes me want to talk differently—with people like him, and like me. Not shout past each other. Not label. To ask: *What are you really afraid of? What do you want to protect?*

Because if we can name that—if we admit it’s not just about borders or jobs, but about dignity, place, respect—then maybe we find common ground.

And Frank? I think he wanted that too. Just never had the words for it.

So thank you… for letting me sit in his chair again.  
For letting me hear him—not as a relic, but as a man trying, in his way, to be fair in an unfair world.  

That matters.  
*He* mattered.
